Female Cave myotis (Myotis velifer) give birth to a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], a reproductive strategy consistent with many temperate vespertilionids that invest heavily in a single offspring annually. Field studies indicate that females typically produce only one litter each year [F_R_i = one litter each year], a low reproductive frequency that is offset by high maternal investment during the gestation and lactation periods. This maximum reproductive output is observed under the stable thermal conditions of maternal roosts, which are maintained at approximately 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], a temperature that supports optimal foetal development and milk synthesis. The energetic demands of maintaining such a thermal regime are substantial, particularly for a small insectivore, and likely constrain the species to a single reproductive event per season. When these thermal conditions are sustained, the observed litter size and annual frequency yield a modest overall reproductive rate that reflects the species' relatively slow life-history pace compared to other bats of comparable body size.

Neonatal female pups of Myotis velifer weigh approximately 3.2 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.2 grams] at birth, a value that represents a substantial proportion of the mother's postpartum body mass and underscores the significant energetic investment in each offspring. This birth mass is typical for newly emerged altricial vespertilionid pups, which are born with closed eyes and sparse pelage but exhibit rapid growth rates during the pre-weaning period. The relatively high birth weight may be an adaptation to the thermal challenges of early life, as heavier neonates possess a greater thermal inertia and can better withstand periodic drops in roost temperature. Comparisons with other members of the genus Myotis reveal that the 3.2 gram birth weight is intermediate, falling between the smaller-bodied Myotis lucifugus and the larger Myotis myotis. This initial mass provides a critical starting point for the rapid somatic development that must occur before the juvenile becomes capable of independent flight and foraging. Adult females go on to attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 11.1 grams [Wwi = approximately 11.1 grams], and field-based mark-recapture studies indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 4124.5 days [am = approximately 4124.5 days] under the same thermal conditions at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C].

Under the thermoneutral conditions typical of an active, euthermic cave myotis, which maintains a core body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], female pups reach sexual maturity at one year after birth [tp = one year after birth], a relatively rapid developmental timeline among bats. This age at puberty is consistent with the species' pattern of autumn mating and spring parturition, as females born in early summer become reproductively active by the following breeding season. Males, in contrast, typically delay maturation until their second year, a common pattern in polygynous or promiscuous bat mating systems where competition for access to females is intense. The attainment of puberty at 365 days after birth is facilitated by the high-quality foraging habitat provided by the species' riparian and desert-scrub environments, which supply abundant insect prey during the summer growing season. This early maturation allows females to begin contributing to population growth within their first calendar year.

Gestation in Myotis velifer proceeds over a period of 65 days [tg = 65 days] when females maintain an elevated roost temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], a duration that places the species within the middle range of gestation lengths reported for temperate-zone vespertilionids. This period encompasses a post-implantation phase during which the embryo undergoes rapid organogenesis and foetal growth, culminating in the delivery of the single relatively large pup. The 65-day gestation is likely sensitive to local thermal conditions, as pregnant females frequently select roost sites with high thermal stability to minimise the energetic costs of thermoregulation. Prolonged periods of cold weather or roost abandonment could delay parturition, though field observations suggest that pregnant females exhibit strong philopatry to thermally suitable caves and abandoned mines. The synchrony between gestation length and seasonal insect abundance ensures that parturition coincides with peak prey availability, maximising the chances of offspring survival through the energetically demanding lactation period.

Lactating female Myotis velifer wean their young after approximately 43 days [tx = approximately 43 days] post-partum, a developmental milestone that marks the transition to nutritional independence in the juvenile at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This weaning age is achieved when mothers maintain a thoracic temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] throughout the nursing period, a thermal regime that optimises milk production and pup growth rates. The 43-day suckling period is relatively extended for a bat of this size, reflecting the energetic constraints of a diet composed exclusively of metabolically dilute insects. During this interval, the pup develops from a 3.2 gram birth-stage individual to a juvenile approaching adult body size, accumulating sufficient lipid reserves to survive overnight foraging excursions. Once weaned, the young bat must quickly learn to capture aerial insect prey, a challenging task that requires the development of echolocation precision and flight maneuverability. Survivorship during the first month after weaning is thought to be lower than at any other life stage, as inexperienced juveniles face high predation risk and frequent foraging failures.
